html:
The Gothic cathedral of Paris, on the Île de la Cité in the Seine. Bishop Maurice de Sully began it in 1163, and most of it was finished by about 1260, with work going on into the 1300s.

It is one of the great works of Gothic architecture. It was among the first buildings to use flying buttresses, outside arches that take the push of the high stone vault, so the walls could be thinner and filled with glass. Its three rose windows and the carved doorways of its west front were models for cathedrals across Europe.

It has seen much of French history. The retrial that cleared Joan of Arc opened there in 1455. In the French Revolution it was looted and made a "Temple of Reason". Napoleon crowned himself emperor there in 1804. Victor Hugo's novel of 1831, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, helped save the decaying building, and Viollet-le-Duc restored it, adding a new spire.

On 15 April 2019 a fire destroyed the roof and spire. The cathedral was rebuilt and reopened in December 2024.
